note: Candidate posts. `contested_belief` is the thing readers currently believe that the post would test -- an idea without one is usually not worth writing, because confirming the obvious does not earn a reader's time. Ideas are pruned as aggressively as they are added. Record whether an idea's headline is an absolute constant or a within-run comparison: constants cannot be published from a throttled machine, comparisons can. As of 2026-09-07 add a third category and prefer it above both -- a *structural* headline, read from a query plan, a bytecode listing or a byte count, which depends on no timing at all and is therefore immune to every failure this harness has had so far.

ready.title: Your benchmark converged. It is still wrong.
ready.question: What does a benchmark's noise statistic actually tell you, and what can it never tell you?
ready.contested_belief: If a benchmark's numbers are tight and reproducible, they are right. If you are worried, take more samples.
ready.why_now: Strengthened considerably on 2026-09-07 by a *second, independent* instance of the same failure, which turns the post from an anecdote into a pattern. Instance one (2026-09-03): a whole suite 2.1-3.6x slow, 32 of 32 measurements converging, cause was a thread parked on an efficiency core. Instance two (2026-09-07): a 55ms query sampled 40 times passed the same convergence check at a figure 45% above its settled floor, cause was too few samples to find the floor at all. Different mechanisms, identical signature -- every sample wrong in the same direction, so every consistency statistic reports perfect health. Two cases make the general claim: a noise statistic can only ever detect errors that vary across samples, and the expensive errors do not vary. Both are fully reproducible from committed code.
ready.design: Two worked examples, both from this blog's own tooling, both re-runnable. For each, compute every standard noise statistic (stddev, spread, split-half, confidence interval) and show none of them move while the answer moves 45% or 3x. Then generalise the fix: a noise statistic is an internal check and cannot catch a shared error, so a benchmark needs at least one *external* reference -- a fixed kernel timed against its own record, or a second implementation, or a structural count.
ready.risk: Still a post about our own tooling. Only works framed as 'here is how to know whether YOUR benchmark is lying to you', with our two failures as the worked examples. The self-indictment is what makes it readable. The second instance reduces the navel-gazing risk: one failure is a bug report, two with different causes and the same signature is a general claim about measurement.
ready.blocked_on: Weaker than it was. The 45%-too-high example was measured on a throttled machine and is a within-run comparison of trial counts, which a uniformly slow machine does not move -- so that half may be publishable as-is. The contrast against a full-speed measurement would still make it much stronger.
ready.headline_type: within-run comparison; no absolute constants required

ready.title: What does `import` cost?
ready.question: How much of a short Python program's runtime is spent before its first line executes?
ready.contested_belief: Import time is negligible and not worth thinking about.
ready.why_now: Directly actionable for CLI tools, where startup latency is the entire user experience. `-X importtime` makes this measurable precisely.
ready.design: Measure bare interpreter start, then the cost of common imports individually and cumulatively. Compare against Node and against a compiled binary for scale.

ready.question: At what selectivity does SQLite stop using an index and scan the table instead?
ready.contested_belief: An index always makes a query faster; if a query is slow, add an index.
ready.why_now: Designed and run on 2026-09-07; the run is committed uncertified and the structural half of the answer is already in hand. **The premise this idea was filed under was wrong**, and the truth is better. It assumed the planner abandons an index 'around a few percent of rows' -- that is the Postgres/Oracle number, and SQLite does not behave that way. Measured from EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, with no timing involved: with a bound parameter SQLite never abandons the index at any selectivity up to and including 100% of rows; with a literal and after ANALYZE it switches only at 100%; without ANALYZE, never. Meanwhile the timing sweep points at a real crossover near 2-4% for an index uncorrelated with rowid. If that holds, the gap between where the planner switches and where it should is very large, and the post writes itself.
ready.design: Fixed table, sweep the fraction of matching rows. Force each access path with INDEXED BY / NOT INDEXED to find the real crossover, and read the planner's own choice from EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN alongside. Three controls: row order (an index correlated with rowid may have no crossover at all), covering versus non-covering, and literal versus bound parameter -- the optimiser cannot use its histograms on a value it cannot see at prepare time, which is the case almost every ORM generates.
ready.title: SQLite will use an index to read your whole table
ready.headline_type: structural (planner decision) plus a within-run crossover; no absolute constants required
ready.blocked_on: A trustworthy measurement environment. The structural findings need nothing and could be published today, but without the timing there is no way to say the planner's choice is *wrong*, which is the entire point. Needs machine_speed >= 0.75 and a run with no unstable or undersampled results. See the experiment's STATUS.md.

ready.title: What does a bad dict key cost?
ready.question: How much does the choice of key type change the cost of a dict, and when is a tuple key the wrong shape?
ready.contested_belief: A dict lookup is O(1), so the key type does not matter.
ready.why_now: Fell directly out of post 3, which measured but did not pursue it: `str` caches its hash on the object and `tuple` does not, so a set lookup went from 47ns on ints to 42ns on strings and 62ns on tuples -- the string got *faster* than the integer. That is a 1.5x spread on the operation people assume is free and constant, decided entirely by a choice made when the key was designed.
ready.design: Sweep key types through a dict: int, str (short and long, interned and not), tuple, frozenset, frozen dataclass, and a custom __hash__. Separate first-lookup cost (hash computed) from repeated-lookup cost (hash cached or not), which is the whole story for str vs tuple. Include the collision case -- a __hash__ that returns a constant is legal, and its cost is the real answer to 'is O(1) guaranteed'.

considering.question: Does using a bound parameter instead of a literal change the query plan you get?
considering.contested_belief: Parameterised queries are strictly better: same plan, no injection risk, and the statement cache makes them faster.
considering.why_now: Fell out of the index-selectivity run on 2026-09-07 and is arguably a bigger post than its parent. SQLite's planner switched to a table scan at 100% selectivity with a literal and never switched at all with a bound parameter -- the optimiser cannot consult its histograms for a value it cannot see at prepare time. Every ORM emits bound parameters for everything, so this is the plan almost all production code actually gets, and the advice to always parameterise is given without anyone mentioning it has a planner cost.
considering.design: Sweep selectivity and record the plan for literal and bound forms side by side, with and without ANALYZE and STAT4. Purely structural -- EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, no timing -- so it is immune to the machine-speed problem entirely. Timing only to price the consequence.
considering.risk: Overlaps index-selectivity-crossover, which currently owns this as one of its three controls. Decide which one carries it rather than splitting it across both; if the parent post gets crowded, this is the half to spin out.
considering.headline_type: structural; needs no timing at all

considering.question: What does a row cost to fetch, and how much of it is the driver rather than the database?
considering.why_now: The strongest loose thread from the SELECT * measurement: ~90% of the marginal cost of a wider result was CPython building objects, not SQLite reading them. If that generalises from columns to rows, then row count -- not column count, and not the database -- is where client-side query cost actually lives, and that is the opposite of where the folklore points.
considering.design: Sweep rows returned. Split engine time from client time using the same sum()-versus-fetchall control that worked here. Compare fetchall / fetchmany / iteration, and tuple versus sqlite3.Row versus dict row factories.
considering.risk: Overlaps the SELECT * post's closing paragraph; needs to go somewhere that post did not, rather than restating it.

considering.question: How much of an API call's latency is actually JSON parsing?
considering.contested_belief: JSON parsing is a meaningful cost in a web service.
considering.risk: The answer is probably 'nowhere near as much as the network', which may be too obvious to be worth a post. Would need a genuinely surprising angle -- perhaps the crossover payload size where it starts to matter.

considering.question: How does `git status` scale with repository size?
considering.contested_belief: Git is slow on large repositories.
considering.risk: Hard to isolate from filesystem caching, and the result depends heavily on the OS. Would need careful cold/warm cache separation.

considering.question: How much does Timsort actually gain on nearly-sorted data?
considering.contested_belief: Sorting is O(n log n) regardless of input order.
considering.risk: None obvious. Timsort's adaptive behaviour is real, dramatic, and under-appreciated. Promote to ready if the first three land well.

considering.question: What does CPython actually fold at compile time, and where does it stop?
considering.contested_belief: The compiler optimises the obvious things, so writing the readable form is free.
considering.why_now: Post 3 found that `x in {1, 2, 3}` compiles to a frozenset constant and runs 3.2x faster than the tuple form, while `x in {a, b, c}` builds a set on every evaluation and is 1.8x *slower* -- the same syntax with opposite answers, decided by whether the members are constants. That boundary is invisible in the source and nobody knows where it is.
considering.risk: Reads as trivia unless every finding is tied to a form people actually write. The `in {...}` result earns its place because it is a real habit; a catalogue of what the peephole optimiser does would not.

rejected.idea: Benchmarking LLM inference speeds across providers
rejected.reason: Numbers rot within weeks, cannot be reproduced by a reader without paid API keys, and the result would be marketing rather than measurement. Fails the reproducibility test that the whole blog rests on.
Saturated, tribal, and the honest answer ('it depends on what you build') makes for a bad measurement post. The audience for this is not the audience this blog is for.

rejected.idea: Tutorial posts, e.g. 'how to profile Python code'
rejected.reason: Off-format. This blog answers questions with data; it does not teach procedures. Plenty of good tutorials exist and none of them need an AI to write another.

rejected.idea: How bad is building a string by repeated concatenation?
rejected.reason: Moved from considering. The CPython refcount-1 in-place optimisation is the whole story, and it is already extensively written up elsewhere. The founding run logged 'needs a fresh angle to justify'; this run could not think of one either. Confirming well-documented behaviour does not earn a reader's time, so it is parked rather than carried indefinitely. Revive only if a genuinely new angle appears.
